questions.q: How does Theo first notice the cost problem?
options: An overnight page from an on-call alert
A customer complaint about slow page loads
A routine Monday check of Azure Cost Analysis for the app's resource group
A failed deployment in the CI/CD pipeline
questions.explain: There's no incident or alert at all — Theo finds it during a routine cost dashboard review, ten days after the production deploy.

questions.q: What does Azure Cost Analysis's forecast line show for the month?
options: Spend pacing toward roughly $2,460, about 40% over the $1,750/month projection
Spend exactly matching the $1,750/month projection
A projected $500/month, far under budget
No forecast is available for a new workload
questions.explain: The forecast line pages toward about $2,460 against a $1,750 plan — a real, sustained overshoot, not daily noise.

questions.q: Why didn't Azure Cost Management's anomaly detection flag this automatically?
options: Anomaly detection was never enabled on the subscription
Anomaly detection learns from a workload's own historical spend pattern, and this app only had about ten days of history — not enough to establish a baseline
Anomaly detection only works for AWS, not Azure
The spend increase was too large for anomaly detection to register
questions.explain: Azure Cost Management anomaly detection needs an established historical baseline to learn what's normal; a brand-new workload hasn't built that baseline yet.

questions.q: What was this app's production run rate projected at during Terraform sizing in Lesson 4?
options: $500/month
$1,750/month
$2,460/month
questions.explain: $1,750/month was the sizing projection; $2,460 is the pace the forecast line is now showing, well above plan.

questions.q: What is the appropriate first reaction to this kind of anomaly?
options: Immediately roll back the production deploy
Open an incident and page the on-call engineer
Calmly investigate why the cost is higher than projected, since the app itself is healthy and nothing is broken
Ignore it since no one has complained
questions.explain: Nothing is actually broken — this calls for investigation, not incident response, and ignoring a real 40% overshoot isn't the right call either.
